notes.heading: Handle step costs and contribution before predicting profit
paragraphs: The straight-line break-even model assumes fixed costs stay fixed over the range studied and that unit contribution remains constant. Additional capacity can introduce a step in fixed costs, while discounts can change the revenue per unit. Calculate each relevant range separately and check whether its proposed break-even output belongs inside that range. Margin of safety compares expected sales with the applicable break-even quantity, and it can shrink even while sales rise. All classroom calculations here use invented businesses and specified prices; they are model exercises rather than forecasts.

questions.prompt: A fictional workshop charges 15 per unit and spends 9 in variable cost per unit. Fixed costs are 600 for output up to 100 units and 900 for output from 101 to 200. Find all whole-number break-even outputs in those ranges.
questions.answer: 100 units in the first range and 150 units in the second.
solution: Solve 600/6=100 and 900/6=150, then verify that each lies in its applicable range.

questions.prompt: A fictional shop has fixed costs 450, price 12 and variable cost 7 per item. Find the minimum whole number of sales for profit of at least 163 units.
questions.answer: 123 sales; profit is 165. At 122 sales profit is 160.
solution: Round up because the goal is a minimum and verify adjacent integers.

questions.prompt: A fictional firm's break-even quantity is 240 and expected sales are 300. Calculate its margin of safety in units and as a percentage of expected sales.
solution: Subtract break-even sales from expected sales: 300-240=60.
Divide by expected sales, not break-even sales: 60/300×100=20.
